thread.title: Scandinavian Festival harbors art, music, tasty food - and stories
thread.title_full: Scandinavian Festival harbors art, music, tasty food - and stories

author: Michael Neary Sun Staff Writer
title: Scandinavian Festival harbors art, music, tasty food - and stories
text:
As Brenda Bard tells it, the Scandinavian Festival in Yuma can strike many different notes, allowing people to share their culture and also to recall some cherished and tasty memories.
“For some it’s remembering grandpas and grandmas and parents – and lutefisk dinners at the Lutheran churches,” she said.
A crowd packed into the ballroom of the Country Roads RV Village in Yuma on Wednesday to celebrate the festival. Throughout the ballroom, people were making foods such as lefse, and they were creating art using techniques such as rosemaling.
On the stage in front, the Yuma Accordion Band was playing, with some members of the Yuma chapter of The Old Time Fiddlers joining in. The band played polkas, rags, foxtrots and a host of other pieces. A Nordic Cafe, meanwhile, was serving open-faced sandwiches, pea soup, meatballs and other foods.
Bard was minding a table at the festival with colorful items and T-shirts sporting her own designs. She pointed to the phrase “Uff da!” inscribed on one of the items.
“It’s an old phrase in Norway,” she said – one that’s taken root in parts of the United States.
Describing the meaning, as Bard explained, takes a little time.
“I refer to it as an expression for life’s little negatives,” she said. “It’s not swearing, but it’s uttered when mishaps occur.”
Burning the cookies, she said, might qualify as an event that elicits an exclamation of “Uff da.”
Bard, as she minded her table, watched and listened to her mother, Ione Bard, playing the accordion along with the other musicians on stage. Brenda Bard, like her mother, is a member of the band. She started playing the accordion about 20 years ago, coming to it as a classical pianist.
Her piano playing, she said, provided some help as she learned the accordion. But she noted deep differences in the sounds of the two instruments.
“The piano technically is a percussion instrument, but the accordion is a wind instrument because it’s full of reeds,” Bard said. “The beauty and the sound and the dynamics come from the bellows.”
Laurie Rye, social-cultural director of the Scandinavian Club of Yuma, said the festival used to be held at the Yuma Civic Center before it was revived, after COVID-19, in the ballroom. The new setting, she said, creates a bit more intimacy.
Rye said the preparation of lefse – described on the Daring Gourmet website as “irresistibly soft, tender and flavorful potato flatbreads” – tends to create a kind of magnet for people at the festival.
“When they can see it demonstrated, when they see how it’s made, they get a good sense of connecting again with those memories with their family,” Rye said.
In another part of the ballroom, Deb Wilson was poring over some wood pieces that she’d prepared for rosemaling – a kind of decorative art that translates as “rose painting.” The creation requires many steps.
“The process starts with a blank piece of wood,” Wilson said. “For me before I start rosemaling, I have to prepare the wood. We put acrylic paint on and then sand it … And then I repaint it and resand it.
“Then I put a glaze on it,” she continued. “And then, depending on what style of painting I’m going to paint, I put the design on with transfer paper.”
Images, Wilson said, might be symmetrical or painted free hand.
“For me the painting is the easiest,” she added. “The most tedious work is to get the wood ready.”
But it’s a necessary series of steps, she said, so that the paint lasts, firmly in place, long after the piece is done.
Rye said the Scandinavian Club of Yuma serves as a big tent, welcoming everyone who’s interested in Scandinavian culture.
“You don’t have to have a drop of Scandinavian blood,” she said, but she added with a chuckle that no one can be too sure that a Scandinavian drop isn’t trickling somewhere.
“The Vikings were everywhere,” she said.
